explain.summary: Nerves carry messages between Kofi's foot and his brain. Sitting on his foot for 40 minutes squashed those nerves, so their signals stopped getting through and the foot felt numb. When he stands, the pressure comes off and blood flows back. The nerves start firing again, but jumbled at first — some too much, some not at all — and his brain reads that as pins and needles until everything is back to normal.
rules: The longer and harder he presses on the foot, the more numb it gets — up to a limit.
After he stands, the numbness halves about every 8 seconds.
Pins and needles rise in the first few seconds, then fade — longer after a longer squash.
A cold floor changes the skin temperature, not the numbness.

source.fact: Many people think a foot falls asleep because blood supply is cut off, but squashed nerves are more to blame: pressure stops them relaying messages to the brain.
As feeling comes back it can feel tingly, like pins and needles, and it lasts only a short time as the connection returns to normal.

Sustained pressure can squeeze arteries and block nerve signals; some nerves stop firing while others fire too much, and the brain reads these mixed signals as tingling — which gets stronger as blood flows back and the nerves restart.
Paresthesia is a burning, tingling or prickling feeling, usually in the hands, arms, legs or feet; nerve injury can come from compression.

choice.what: Numbness builds up with a 15-minute half-time
choice.why: Chosen so 10 minutes gives mild numbness and 40 minutes strong numbness, matching the story.

choice.what: Numbness halves every 8 seconds after standing; tingling fades over about a minute
choice.why: Sources say the tingling is short; we made it longer after a longer squash, as clue 4 describes.

choice.what: Weight and fidgeting scale the squash
choice.why: More pressure squashes nerves harder and shifting gives relief; the exact amounts vary.

choice.what: Floor temperature only changes skin temperature
choice.why: This is how the model tests the cold-foot idea.

illustrative: Kofi is fictional; the 0–10 numbness and tingling scales are made-up scales.
His skin temperature of about 88°F is a typical value, not a measurement.

does: Shows numbness building the longer a nerve is squashed
Shows the pins-and-needles phase as the nerve restarts
Lets you test whether a cold floor could be the cause
doesnt: Measure any real person — Kofi is fictional and the numbers are illustrative
Separate nerve squashing from blood-flow squashing
Cover numbness or tingling that happens without pressure
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Numbness or tingling that happens without sitting on something, or doesn't go away, is a reason to tell an adult.
